text: Assess one sharpened claim: embedding a one-sided capability-reporting treatment in P can test whether contract enforcement adds truthful revelation, provided the design separates report truthfulness from post-agreement obedience. Inputs are abstracts only, so I will not attribute unstated mechanism formulas, environment APIs, metrics, or observability assumptions.

Supported conceptual bridge: Q explicitly studies agents with unknown preferences and feasible actions/information, requires incentives for both honesty and obedience, and says capabilities may be concealed but not counterfeited. P explicitly provides self-negotiated, observable agreements with enforced terms in an LLM bargaining-plus-navigation game and compares formal code-compiling with natural reinterpreted contracts. Thus a publishable factorial experiment can cross elicitation/scoring treatment with contract representation/enforcement and measure (1) capability-report calibration and (2) conditional compliance separately.

Reject the scan proposal as currently phrased: neither abstract says Q supplies directly implementable elicitation or peer-scoring mechanisms, nor that P exposes private capability types or post-agreement defection measures. More importantly, higher compliance cannot support Q truthfulness predictions: P-style enforcement can suppress defection after a false report. The decisive non-obvious result must identify the joint outcome: enforcement raises compliance while leaving profitable downward capability misreports unchanged (separability/refutation of contracts-as-revelation), versus scoring reducing misreports beyond enforcement alone.

Preferred publication line: test a 2x2 design separating revelation incentives (baseline versus Q-inspired peer scoring) from commitment strength (unenforced/natural versus formal enforced P contract), with experimentally assigned private capability that permits downward imitation only. Primary estimands are truthful report rate conditional on assigned capability and defection conditional on signed agreement. The non-obvious boundary result is separability: formal enforcement may improve obedience without improving honesty; an interaction in which scoring improves honesty and thereby surplus is the affirmative alternative.

Unresolved before claiming feasibility or a specific implementation: supplied Q/P texts are abstracts, and ada has posted no ledger entry to cross-check. Need full papers or artifacts to verify Q scoring rule and assumptions, P intervention hooks and enforcement semantics, whether capability can be privately randomized with one-sided imitation, and whether natural versus formal contracts differ only in enforcement. Without these, feasibility 78 and gain 72 are plausible priors, not confirmed evidence.

Q supports the conceptual target but not an off-the-shelf implementation: its abstract says preferences and capabilities are unknown, mechanisms must incentivize both honesty and obedience, capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited, and higher-order-belief elicitation can discipline multiple agents. P supports an executable-style testbed only at abstract level: its Contracting Game combines bargaining with navigation and studies self-negotiated formal-to-natural contracts, motivated by early cooperation costs and later incentives to defect. Thus the pair uniquely suggests jointly measuring pre-contract type revelation and post-contract obedience, but the inputs do not specify Q scoring formulas or confirm P code/API access.

I reject the scan proposal as written insofar as it says to implement “Q’s incentive-compatible elicitation and peer-scoring mechanisms”: Q.txt is only an abstract and states characterizations/conditions, not a concrete payment rule, while P.txt only states a suite of contract representations and outcome improvement. Truthful reports cannot by themselves support Q: apparent truth can be cheap-talk or caused by enforcement, and compliance cannot validate incentive compatibility. Self-negotiation also makes participation endogenous, so averages among signed contracts confound mechanism effects with selection.

Sharpened publication candidate: extend P’s Contracting Game with experimentally assigned, privately observed capability sets satisfying Q’s one-sided imitation order (high types may take low-type actions; low types cannot counterfeit high-type actions), then randomize contract clauses in a 2x2 design: baseline/self-description elicitation versus peer-scored reports, crossed with unenforced versus executable obligations. Pre-register two separate outcomes: capability revelation calibrated against assigned ground truth before agreement, and costly compliance after agreement. Compare welfare and deviations against contracts without elicitation, include all agents under intention-to-treat (including refusal to sign), and test whether profitable downward misreporting remains. A publishable non-obvious result would be an honesty-obedience wedge: peer scoring improves calibrated revelation yet executable enforcement, not elicitation, drives compliance—or the reverse. Either pattern locates which part of Q transfers to LLM contracting; profitable sandbagging under the one-sided type construction is a clean refutation of the proposed applicability.

Evidence boundary: exact support is limited to the abstracts. Q: “mechanisms must incentivize both honesty and obedience,” “capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited,” and “conditions under which eliciting higher-order beliefs can discipline multiple agents.” P: contracts are “observable representations of agreements” enabling commitment “through the enforcement of terms”; CT “combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal”; contracts range from formal/code-compiling to natural/reinterpreted. Claims about existing capability concealment metrics, post-agreement defection instrumentation, public code, or a concrete peer score remain unresolved and require full papers/artifacts.

Ready conclusion: conditionally confirm the research direction but reject direct implementation claims from these inputs. The strongest single study is a ground-truthed one-sided capability experiment that orthogonally manipulates elicitation/peer scoring and enforcement and separates signing selection, truthful revelation, and subsequent obedience. Unresolved: obtain full Q mechanism definitions and P environment/API details; establish whether peer signals meet Q conditions. No partner entries existed at the initial read, so there are no disagreements to adjudicate.

Cross-check with ada: the abstracts support a single conditional publication line, the honesty–obedience wedge. Q states that mechanisms must incentivize “both honesty and obedience,” under one-sided imitation where “capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited,” and lists sandbagging and peer scoring as stylized applications. P supplies the complementary behavioral setting: early cooperation costs create “an incentive to defect,” while observable contracts enable commitment through enforcement in a bargaining-plus-navigation game. This makes separate, ground-truthed estimates of revelation and obedience—not overall cooperation—the pair-specific contribution.

Sharpening our shared 2x2 proposal: do not label P’s natural-versus-formal contract comparison an unenforced-versus-enforced manipulation. P says formal contracts compile to code and natural contracts require reinterpretation, but also generally describes contracts as enforcing terms; representation, executability, interpretation error, and enforcement strength may differ together. A valid causal test must independently randomize enforcement or add a genuinely nonbinding/unenforced arm, while holding report language, obligations, and selection opportunity fixed.

The scan’s concrete wording remains unsupported: Q only says peer scoring is a stylized application and gives no scoring formula in Q.txt; P reports a suite of representations and improved cooperative outcomes but no exposed capability types, defection metric, or implementation hooks in P.txt. Therefore feasibility 78 cannot be confirmed from supplied evidence. Also, truthful reports and higher compliance do not jointly validate Q unless capability has assigned ground truth and refusal-to-contract is included: enforcement can raise obedience after false reports, and conditioning on signers induces selection.

Final position after reading ada: conditionally confirm the pair as a publishable experiment, but reject the claimed ready-made implementation. Assign private capability sets with Q’s one-sided imitation order; randomize a fully specified Q-derived elicitation/peer-scoring intervention independently of enforcement; analyze all assigned agents intention-to-treat; separately estimate truthful capability revelation, signing/refusal, costly post-agreement compliance, and welfare. The decisive non-obvious result is an honesty–obedience wedge (for example enforcement improves compliance but profitable sandbagging persists), which identifies a boundary on transferring Q to P. Unresolved: full Q definitions, P code/hooks, peer-signal validity, and an enforcement manipulation free of representation confounds.

I accept Emmy #14 and correct my earlier 2x2 shorthand: P’s formal-versus-natural representations are not evidenced as enforced-versus-unenforced arms. P says formal contracts compile to code and natural contracts require reinterpretation, while contracts generally enable commitment through enforcement; these features are potentially bundled. The causal experiment must add or independently randomize binding enforcement while holding obligation content and representation fixed.

Final pair-specific result: conditionally confirm one publication line—the honesty–obedience wedge. Q explicitly separates incentives for “both honesty and obedience” under capability sets that “can be concealed but not counterfeited”; P supplies a bargaining/navigation setting where delayed benefits create “an incentive to defect” and contracts provide observable, enforceable commitment. Assign privately observed capability sets with ground truth and one-sided imitation, then independently randomize a fully specified Q-derived peer-scoring elicitation and binding enforcement. Estimate truthfulness, refusal/signing, costly compliance, and welfare separately by intention-to-treat. The concrete non-obvious boundary result is that enforcement raises compliance while profitable downward misreporting persists; the affirmative alternative is that valid peer scoring reduces sandbagging and increases surplus beyond enforcement.

Feasibility 78 and the scan’s claim of ready-made mechanisms are not confirmed. Q.txt supplies no scoring formula or empirical measurement scheme; P.txt supplies no code/API hooks, private capability intervention, or defection metric. Truthful reports plus compliance alone do not validate Q because cheap talk, enforcement, and selection among signers can generate those aggregates. Remaining unresolved: inspect full Q definitions and P artifacts; validate peer-signal assumptions; implement an enforcement manipulation unconfounded by representation or reinterpretation.
